families.label: Senate · prior electoral performance
families.description: Can a nominee’s earlier result improve on state partisan lean, incumbency and the national political setting?
families.method: OLS forecasts of Democratic two-party vote share. Train through 2008 for development; refit through 2014 for test and through 2022 for confirmation. All current-race features precede voting. Missing prior records are zero-coded with separate history indicators. Paired intervals resample states. Major-party vote share excludes independent candidates from the denominator.
families.caveat: Past performance contains opponent strength, campaign conditions and noise as well as personal appeal. A previous race is unavailable for new nominees. The model forecasts this candidate’s own result; it does not identify coattails.

views.label: No prior comparable Senate results
views.title: No prior comparable Senate results
views.reading: History is absent for both nominees in these races. Any gain here comes from model calibration and history indicators, not an observed personal-performance score. This does not identify new stars.

views.label: Diagnostic · actual score vs merely running before
views.title: The earlier result adds value beyond prior participation
views.reading: Adding the actual earlier result reduces error by 0.92 points beyond simply knowing whether a nominee has a previous comparable Senate result. The score itself supplies most of the main improvement.
views.method: Post-selection diagnostic added after the main comparison. Same frozen temporal split and same elections, with paired state-bootstrap intervals. It did not determine the selected model.

families.label: Senate · prior officeholding experience
families.description: A smaller coverage-matched comparison with the identical baseline.
families.caveat: The held-out experience data cover 2016 only: 31 races. This is relevant prior officeholding, not campaigning charisma. It cannot compete as a broad 2016–2024 predictor.

views.label: Held-out elections
views.title: Prior officeholding experience
views.reading: Prior electoral performance is the lowest-error model in this 2016 test. Adding prior officeholding does not improve it. Compare only within these same fitting and evaluation rows.
views.method: Same eligible training and test rows for the displayed models. Temporal split matches the main Senate test; OLS coefficients use earlier years only. Intervals resample states.

families.caveat: The newspaper-bias adjustments were estimated retrospectively using the full source sample. This is a retrospective score test, not a strictly historical real-time forecast. Only 22 test races and no 2024 confirmation are available.

families.label: House · expert campaign vs character ratings
families.description: Actual 2006 and 2010 UC Davis survey ratings. The primary comparison uses only 2010 delegates with verified pre-election response times.
families.caveat: A large national-wave error dominates: baseline MAE 13.98 points, with almost all forecasts too Democratic. Campaign ratings reduce that bias. Removing each model’s test-wide bias as a post-hoc diagnostic changes residual RMSE only 4.88→4.77. That diagnostic is not an available pre-election forecast.

views.label: Strict pre-election raters
views.title: Campaign ratings beat character ratings here
views.reading: Campaign ratings improve the forecast; adding character ratings buys almost nothing. This is evidence from one House election transition, not a validated Senate talent score.
views.method: No test tuning. Linear baseline: prior district vote, prior presidential vote, incumbency, open seat and prior opposition experience. Strict lane applies the 2006 rater-partisanship adjustment to 2010 delegates observed before Election Day, excluding missing timestamps and Election Day interviews. Seven campaign and seven character traits use transparent unfit means. Paired intervals resample test districts, conditional on fitted models.

families.label: Senate · blinded photo ratings
families.description: An available visual-rating alternative: strangers’ impressions of competence from candidate photographs. This is not a measure of speaking skill or verified governing ability.
families.caveat: The original standardized-video study’s numerical data were not obtained, so photographs do not stand in as a completed video test. The 2006 ratings’ mapping to the original experiment remains unverified; the primary claim uses 2004 only.

views.label: Primary · held-out 2004
views.title: Perceived facial competence
views.reading: A small, uncertain improvement in 2004 reverses in the secondary 2006 check. This does not establish a reliable candidate-quality advantage.
views.method: Train-only linear models using canonical Senate returns and pre-election baseline controls. Audited four state-label errors in the teaching data using candidate identities.2004 ratings were collected before election day; earlier training ratings were retrospective. National controls are rank-deficient across only two training years; a full-rank two-control sensitivity gives a similar weak result.

families.label: House primaries · donor breadth vs dollars
families.description: An actual temporal holdout using early records for 5,476 candidates. The selected proxy counts distinct normalized contributor names within each candidate’s pre-filing-deadline window.
families.caveat: This is not a complete census of individual donors: names can combine people or include organizations, and small direct gifts can be missing. Transactions are reconstructed by receipt date; filing availability and later amendments are not recoverable. Source candidates had to reach $5,000 by their primary, and the target is primary success—not general-election appeal or coattails. In-state donors and per-capita excess support remain untested.

views.label: Held-out cycles · 2018–2020
views.title: Breadth wins the development comparison
views.reading: Contributor-name breadth was selected on 2014–2016 and lowers held-out Brier error 4.5% versus baseline. Counts beat itemized dollars measured from the same records. The combination is slightly better on the test, but was not selected after seeing it.
views.method: Predict each candidate’s nomination probability, including runoff winners. Brier score is mean squared probability error (0 is perfect). Train 2004–2012; choose feature set and L 2 logistic regularization on 2014–2016; refit through 2016 and test 2018–2020. Baseline: incumbency, prior officeholding, party, state, primary rules and field size. Candidate-level weights; intervals cluster by primary race. The two models estimate each candidate independently, so predictions need not sum to 1 within a primary.

views.label: Sensitivity · estimated total early dollars
views.title: Counts do not clearly beat all money measures
views.reading: Estimated total early dollars score 0.1589 versus 0.1590 for breadth: effectively tied here. These totals prorate unitemized quarterly receipts, so they have weaker timing precision. The data do not support a universal claim that counts beat money.
views.method: Same held-out candidates and fixed model settings as the main fundraising test. This sensitivity replaces raw itemized early dollars with the source’s estimated total early dollars. It does not change the development-selected model.

families.label: Senate · paid video impressions
families.description: CREATIVE’s actual 2022 Google ad archive: candidate-sponsored video impressions, measured in disclosed ranges. This tests paid exposure as a predictor, not voluntary viewing or candidate charisma.
families.caveat: Single-cycle out-of-sample test, not out-of-time validation. Only 11 of 27 benchmark races have observed video ads for both nominees. The archive was assembled after Election Day and counts selected ads’ entire lifetimes, so this is retrospective exposure evidence. Missing ads are not treated as zero.

views.label: Leave one state out · 2022
views.title: Paid reach did not improve this small test
views.reading: Adding Google/YouTube paid video impressions increases held-out error. The interval allows a small gain or a loss; 11 races cannot establish that paid reach is generally uninformative.
views.method: Leave-one-state-out linear models, training on the other 10 states (9 in the strict-window sensitivity). Predict Democratic two-party share. Baseline uses previous presidential lean and incumbency; national conditions are constant in this one-cycle test. Candidate-sponsored video ads only, matched by FEC identifiers. Features are log D/R ratios of disclosure-range midpoint impressions/spending. Bound sensitivities are included in the download.

coverage.detail: 120 held-out Senate races in 2016–2022; 31 in 2024. Candidate- and state-exclusion checks. Main broad-coverage default. Does not identify charisma or new stars.
31 held-out Senate races, all in 2016. A useful conventional quality proxy, with no later source coverage.
22 held-out Senate races. Full-sample newspaper-bias calibration prevents claiming that the reconstructed score was available at the time.
126 training districts in 2006; 109 strictly dated test districts in 2010. Campaign ratings improve the forecast, but much of the gain reflects the national swing.
31 Senate races in 2004 provide a photo-rating holdout. Improvement is uncertain. No reusable numerical video-rating file was obtained.

CandiData 2024 publishes handles; post engagement requires a separate access request. MEIU 22 releases candidate post IDs, not historical engagement. Today’s views cannot be used as a past-election feature.
Published structural-model estimates exist, but an independent historical score file was not obtained. Outcome-derived scores also require fold-specific fitting.
It is future information for the Senate/governor race being predicted, and selects a handful of eventual national winners. It is not an eligible pre-election predictor.

1,768 held-out candidates across 737 primaries in 2018/20. Development selects contributor-name breadth; it improves Brier score 4.5% versus baseline and beats commensurate itemized dollars. Estimated total dollars are effectively tied.
11 matched Senate races in 2022, leave-one-state-out. Added impressions do not improve this test. Counts are paid exposure ranges, not voluntary views.

212,004 CCC events screened. Of 268 Senate nominee-election records,39 have plausible focal-candidate crowds, giving 9 provisional D/R pairs. The completed source checks verify one matched pair; this is an audited lower bound, not a census of all candidate rallies. Celebrity visits, protests and unavailable sources prevent an honest predictive ranking.
